common_name: Gypsy Queen Chrysanthemum (Bronze Spider-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant rooted spring cuttings after frost in full sun; grow as a single disbudded stem and stake early to support the heavy bronze spider bloom.

directions: Gypsy Queen is a late-season spider-type exhibition chrysanthemum whose long, fine bronze ray florets radiate outward from an open center and curl into tight hooks at their tips, producing the loose, airy silhouette spider mums are prized for. Disbud the plant to a single terminal bud in late summer so the bloom can develop its full span, and tie the heavy flower head to a cane well before it opens since the slender stem cannot support it unaided. Take basal cuttings from stock plants each winter under glass, since spider-type blooms lose their characteristic length and hook when grown from old, woody clumps rather than vigorous young growth. Protect overwintering stock from hard freezes; this cultivar is maintained as a disbud exhibition plant rather than left outdoors as a garden perennial.
sources: National Chrysanthemum Society (USA) — Bloom Finder (2021 Edition)

common_name: Fairy Lace Chrysanthemum (White Spider-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Set out spring cuttings after frost danger passes; disbud to one stem and shield the delicate white spider florets from hard rain.

directions: Fairy Lace is a mid-season spider-type exhibition mum with slender, pure white tubular florets that coil delicately at the tips, giving the open bloom a lace-like, airy texture distinct from the denser incurve and reflex classes. Grow it as a disbudded single stem, pinching once to establish the plant and then removing every lateral bud so all of the plant's energy drives one large terminal flower. Stake the stem early, since the wide-spreading bloom becomes top-heavy as the florets fully extend, and shield the white petals from direct rain and strong sun to keep their color from browning at the edges. Propagate from fresh cuttings taken off overwintered stock plants rather than from divided clumps to keep the characteristic fine, curling floret form.
sources: National Chrysanthemum Society (USA) — Bloom Finder (2021 Edition)

planting.note: Transplant spring cuttings once frost has passed; disbud to a single stem and stake well ahead of the heavy, late-opening purple spider bloom.

directions: Windchime is a late-season spider-type exhibition chrysanthemum bearing long, lavender-purple tubular florets that hook and twist at their tips, creating the loosely radiating movement that gives the cultivar its name. As with other disbud spider types, limit the plant to one terminal bud by removing all side shoots through summer, and stake the stem well ahead of bloom since the extended florets add considerable weight and leverage to the flower head. Because the long growing season needed to finish a full-sized bloom often runs past the first frost in cooler climates, exhibitors commonly finish Windchime under cold-frame or greenhouse cover. Keep propagation going from basal cuttings each year rather than relying on an aging clump, which tends to produce shorter, less defined florets.
sources: National Chrysanthemum Society (USA) — Bloom Finder (2021 Edition)

common_name: Goldfinger Chrysanthemum (Seaton's Goldfinger, Bronze Spider-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant spring cuttings after last frost in full sun; disbud to one stem and stake early to carry the tightly coiled bronze spider bloom.

directions: Goldfinger, also listed in NCS records as Seaton's Goldfinger, is a late-season bronze spider-type exhibition mum whose narrow, strongly hooked florets curve back toward the stem in the tight spiral exhibitors look for in top-quality spider blooms. Disbud to a single stem in mid-to-late summer and support the stem with a cane well before the bud swells, since the dense coil of florets concentrates considerable weight at the head. Because the cultivar needs a long, cool finishing season to develop its full curl and size, growers in short-season climates typically time the final pinch to push bloom into late autumn under cover. Renew stock from basal cuttings annually; divided old clumps rarely reproduce the tightly coiled floret form reliably.
sources: National Chrysanthemum Society (USA) — Bloom Finder (2021 Edition)

common_name: Fire Wheel Chrysanthemum (Red Spoon-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Set spring cuttings in full sun after frost; disbud to a single stem and stake to support the red spoon-form bloom.

directions: Fire Wheel is a mid-season spoon-type exhibition chrysanthemum whose narrow red tubular ray florets open into small flattened, spoon-shaped tips, spinning outward from the bloom's center like the spokes the cultivar is named for. Grow it as a disbudded single stem, removing side buds as they form so the plant's energy concentrates in one well-formed flower, and stake the stem since spoon-type blooms can be top-heavy despite their moderate size. Because the distinctive spoon tips show their best color and form on vigorous young growth, propagate annually from basal cuttings taken off overwintered stock rather than from an undivided clump. Shelter stock plants from hard freezes over winter where grown outside the warmer end of its hardiness range.
sources: National Chrysanthemum Society (USA) — Bloom Finder (2021 Edition)

planting.note: Transplant spring cuttings after frost; disbud to one stem and stake early for the large red spoon bloom.

directions: Redwing is a late-season spoon-type exhibition mum with larger, deep red florets that flare into distinct spatulate tips, giving the bloom a bold, wheel-like form at the upper end of the spoon class's size range. Pinch the young plant once to set its form, then disbud to a single terminal flower and stake the stem early, since the broad spoon-tipped florets add noticeable weight as the bloom opens fully. A long, cool finishing season brings out the best floret length and color, so growers in shorter-season climates often protect late-blooming stems under cover as autumn closes in. Keep a fresh cutting cycle going each winter, since the clean spoon shape fades in plants left to clump and age.
sources: National Chrysanthemum Society (USA) — Bloom Finder (2021 Edition)

planting.note: Plant spring cuttings after frost in fertile soil; disbud to one stem for this early-flowering pink spoon mum.

directions: Centerpiece is an early-flowering spoon-type exhibition chrysanthemum, its soft pink tubular florets opening wide into neat, flattened spoon tips arranged in orderly spokes around the bloom's center. Because it finishes earlier than most exhibition classes, it suits growers in shorter-season climates who want a spoon-type bloom without pushing the plant into late autumn; disbud to one terminal bud and support the stem with a stake as the bloom approaches full size. Take fresh basal cuttings from overwintered stock each year, since Centerpiece's defined spoon shape and clear pink color are best expressed on young, vigorously growing wood. Grow in full sun and evenly moist, well-drained soil, feeding regularly through the growing season to support the disbud's single large flower.
sources: National Chrysanthemum Society (USA) — Bloom Finder (2021 Edition)

planting.note: Set out spring cuttings after frost; disbud to a single stem and finish in cool autumn weather for best green color.

directions: Shamrock is a mid-season quill-type exhibition chrysanthemum named for its unusual chartreuse-green to yellow-green coloring, with straight, tubular florets that stay closed or just barely open at the tip rather than curling or spooning. Disbud the plant to a single stem and remove all side buds through the season so the fully double, quill-petaled bloom can reach its full size, staking the stem as the heavy flower head develops. The cool, unusual green tone is most pronounced when the plant finishes in cool autumn conditions, so growers in warm climates often get the best color by timing the final disbud for a late bloom. Propagate from basal cuttings taken off overwintered stock each winter rather than old clumps, which tend to lose bloom size and color intensity.
sources: National Chrysanthemum Society (USA) — Bloom Finder (2021 Edition)

planting.note: Plant spring cuttings after frost danger passes; disbud to one stem and stake for the dense bronze quill bloom.

directions: Honey is a mid-season quill-type exhibition mum with straight, tubular bronze florets that stay tightly closed through most of their length, giving the fully double bloom a dense, pin-cushion texture quite different from the open-faced quill cultivars. Grow it as a disbudded single stem, pinching once early in the season and removing every side shoot afterward so the plant's full vigor goes into one terminal flower, with staking in place well before the bud swells. Because quill-type blooms show their straightest, most uniform florets on strong young growth, renew the stock plant each year from basal cuttings rather than letting an old clump carry over. Overwinter stock under glass or in a cold frame in regions where winters are severe.
sources: National Chrysanthemum Society (USA) — Bloom Finder (2021 Edition)

common_name: King's Delight Chrysanthemum (Pink Quill-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Transplant spring cuttings after frost in rich soil; disbud to a single stem and stake the heavy pink quill bloom.

directions: King's Delight is a mid-season pink quill-type exhibition chrysanthemum whose straight, tubular florets open just enough at the tip to reveal a lighter obverse color, producing a soft two-toned effect across the fully double bloom. As with other large quill types, disbud to a single stem and stake it early, since the dense arrangement of tubular florets makes for a heavy, top-loaded flower head once fully open. Take basal cuttings annually from overwintered stock to maintain the straight, well-filled quill form, since clump-grown plants tend to produce shorter, less uniform florets. Site the plant in full sun with rich, well-drained soil and consistent moisture through summer to support strong disbud growth.
sources: National Chrysanthemum Society (USA) — Bloom Finder (2021 Edition)

planting.note: Plant spring cuttings after frost; pinch for multiple spray stems rather than disbudding this fine-petaled yellow brush-type mum.

directions: Cisco is a late-season yellow chrysanthemum of the brush-and-thistle class, its very fine tubular ray florets standing upright in the brush style rather than drooping outward, which gives the medium-sized bloom a dense, bristly texture unlike any of the broader-petaled exhibition classes. Because brush-and-thistle types are grown mainly as spray or specialty blooms for classification shows, pinch the young plant to encourage several flowering stems rather than disbudding to a single giant bloom. Keep the plant staked as the fine-textured flower heads open, since the narrow florets are easily damaged by wind and rain. Renew the planting from basal cuttings each year, since this uncommon bloom class is maintained almost entirely through cutting propagation among specialist growers.
sources: National Chrysanthemum Society (USA) — Bloom Finder (2021 Edition)

common_name: Saga No Yuki Chrysanthemum (White Brush-and-Thistle-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Set spring cuttings in a sheltered, full-sun spot; train as a pinched spray rather than a single disbud for this small white thistle-type bloom.

directions: Saga No Yuki is a late-season white brush-and-thistle chrysanthemum in the Japanese Saga style, its very fine, upright tubular florets forming a small, snow-white, bristle-textured bloom under two inches across that nearly conceals the central disk florets. Grow it as a spray-trained plant with several pinched stems rather than a single disbud, since the small individual blooms are meant to be displayed in clusters in the brush-and-thistle class. Site plants in full sun with sheltered footing, since the fine florets bruise easily in wind and heavy rain. Propagate from basal cuttings each winter, as this specialty Japanese bloom type is kept true to form almost exclusively through vegetative cutting propagation rather than from seed or old clumps.
sources: National Chrysanthemum Society (USA) — Bloom Finder (2021 Edition)

planting.note: Transplant spring cuttings after frost in a wind-sheltered spot; pinch for spray-grown purple brush-type blooms.

directions: Aoi is a late-season purple brush-and-thistle chrysanthemum whose fine, upright tubular florets stand stiffly together to form a small, dense, bristle-like bloom characteristic of the Japanese brush style within this specialty exhibition class. Train the plant to several pinched stems for spray display rather than disbudding to one giant flower, since brush-and-thistle types are traditionally shown as clustered sprays of small, uniform blooms. Protect the fine florets from wind and heavy rain, which easily flatten or bruise the narrow, upright petals before the bloom fully matures. Keep the planting going from basal cuttings taken off overwintered stock each year, since this uncommon class is maintained almost entirely through cutting propagation among NCS specialty growers.
sources: National Chrysanthemum Society (USA) — Bloom Finder (2021 Edition)

common_name: Flying Saucer Chrysanthemum (White Anemone-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Plant spring cuttings after frost in rich soil; disbud to one stem and stake early for the broad white anemone bloom.

directions: Flying Saucer is a late-season white anemone-type exhibition chrysanthemum, its short, broad outer ray florets forming a flat white collar around a prominently raised, cushion-like central disk of elongated disk florets, the defining two-tiered look of the anemone class. Disbud the plant to a single terminal bud and stake it early, since the wide flat guard petals combined with the raised center make for an unusually broad, heavy flower head. Because the raised center disk develops its fullest, most rounded shape on vigorous new growth, propagate annually from basal cuttings rather than old clumps, which tend to produce flatter, less distinct centers. Grow in full sun and rich, evenly moist soil, feeding through the season to support strong disbud development.
sources: National Chrysanthemum Society (USA) — Bloom Finder (2021 Edition)

common_name: Powder Puff Chrysanthemum (White Anemone-Type Exhibition Mum)

planting.note: Set out spring cuttings after frost; disbud to a single stem and water evenly to keep the raised white center symmetrical.

directions: Powder Puff is a late-season white anemone-type exhibition mum whose short, rounded outer florets form a neat collar around a tall, densely packed cushion of disk florets, giving the bloom the soft, rounded look its name describes. Pinch once to establish the plant, then disbud to a single stem so the raised center can develop its full height and roundness, staking the stem well before the heavy flower head opens. The prominent cushion center is best formed on strong, actively growing wood, so take fresh basal cuttings from overwintered stock each winter rather than propagating from an aging clump. Provide full sun and consistent moisture through the growing season, since uneven watering can cause the raised center to form unevenly or flatten on one side.
sources: National Chrysanthemum Society (USA) — Bloom Finder (2021 Edition)
